Disappointed by Lack of Respect and Unprofessional Community Management

I am writing this review with great disappointment, not regarding the gameplay mechanics of Hearts of Iron IV itself, but because of the unacceptable behavior occurring within the official Paradox Interactive Discord server.

Recently, an official moderator representing Paradox Interactive made disrespectful and insulting remarks toward Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder of the Republic of Türkiye and one of the most prominent historic figures featured in this very game.

Hearts of Iron IV is a historical strategy game that relies heavily on historical accuracy, respect for nations, and an engaged global community. It is deeply ironic and hypocritical that a game featuring historical leaders is moderated by individuals who openly disrespect them and insult the national values of players. Representatives of a major game studio should uphold professional standards, neutrality, and basic human decency. Allowing community managers or moderators to engage in hate speech or offensive behavior completely ruins the trust between the developers and the player base.

As a loyal player who has supported Paradox for a long time, I cannot overlook such toxic and unprofessional behavior from official staff. Players deserve a safe, respectful, and unbiased environment on official platforms.

Until Paradox Interactive takes action regarding its moderation team and enforces a zero-tolerance policy against disrespect toward historical figures and national values, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game or support the studio.

Paradox Interactive's recent attitude towards the Turkish community is deeply disappointing and unacceptable.

Hearts of Iron IV is a game built around history, historical figures, nations, and the events that shaped the modern world. Yet when it comes to Turkish players and Gazi Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the standards suddenly seem to be different.

Atatürk was the founder of the Republic of Türkiye and the leader of the Turkish War of Independence. Regardless of anyone's personal political views, he is an undeniably important historical figure whose image and legacy are deeply significant to millions of Turkish people.

The fact that a player was banned for using Atatürk's image, while Paradox's games freely portray countless historical leaders and controversial figures, raises serious questions about consistency and double standards.

This is not simply about one player or one profile picture. It is about how a company that makes money by turning history into entertainment chooses to treat one of its largest and most dedicated player communities.

Turkish players have supported Paradox games for years, yet Turkish language support is still absent from Hearts of Iron IV. And now we are expected to simply accept what many Turkish players see as disrespect towards one of the most important figures in our history.

I have spent hundreds of hours playing this game, but supporting a game is not just about its gameplay. It is also about the company behind it and how that company treats its community.

If you are going to build games around history, then you should at least show consistency and respect when dealing with the people and historical figures represented in that history.

Until Paradox addresses this situation clearly and treats the Turkish community with the same consistency and respect as everyone else, I cannot recommend Hearts of Iron IV.

I am submitting a formal complaint regarding what I consider to be an extremely serious case of discriminatory, politically biased and inconsistent moderation associated with Paradox Interactive’s official community.

A Turkish user was reportedly punished for using a portrait of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and first President of the Republic of Türkiye, as a profile picture. According to the moderation exchange that has been publicly shared, the user was told that Atatürk was considered a “controversial figure,” and the moderator attempted to associate him with the events of 1915 as part of the justification for the punishment.

This is completely unacceptable.

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk is not an extremist symbol, a hate symbol or an inherently prohibited political symbol. He is the founder of the modern Republic of Türkiye and one of the most important figures in Turkish history.

A private company or an individual community moderator does not have the right to arbitrarily treat the portrait of Atatürk as though displaying it is, by itself, misconduct deserving punishment.

The situation becomes even more disturbing when other controversial historical leaders, military figures and political personalities appear to be tolerated while Atatürk is selectively targeted.

If one historical figure is prohibited because somebody considers that person “controversial,” while comparable or considerably more controversial figures are allowed, this is not neutral moderation. It is selective enforcement.

Furthermore, the wording reportedly used by the moderator raises serious concerns that personal political or ideological views may be influencing moderation decisions.

For Turkish users, this is not merely an argument about a Discord profile picture.

A moderator representing an official community appears to have taken a disputed historical and political narrative, treated it as sufficient justification to target the portrait of the founder of Türkiye, and then punished a Turkish player on that basis.

This creates the appearance of ideological bias and raises legitimate questions about whether external political narratives, lobbying, or individual activist positions are influencing moderation decisions inside Paradox communities.

I am therefore asking Valve to investigate this matter rather than dismiss it as an ordinary disagreement between a moderator and a user.

In particular, I ask Valve to examine:

• Whether users are being punished specifically for displaying images of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

• Whether comparable rules are being applied equally to users displaying other historical and political figures.

• Whether Paradox moderators are introducing their own political interpretations into community moderation.

• Whether Turkish users have been subjected to selective enforcement, removal of objections, bans or other unequal treatment during this controversy.

• Whether the moderation policies associated with a major publisher operating through Steam are being applied consistently and without discrimination based on nationality or national identity.

This controversy has understandably caused enormous anger among Turkish players.

The issue is not that Atatürk must be protected from historical discussion or criticism. Historical debate is legitimate.

The issue is that a moderator should not be allowed to transform their own disputed political interpretation into a moderation rule and then use that rule to punish players.

Atatürk should not be treated as a criminal, extremist symbol or prohibited figure simply because an individual moderator — or any political pressure group — objects to him.

Turkish players deserve exactly the same treatment, respect and moderation standards as every other community on Steam.

If Paradox Interactive permits this kind of selective enforcement in an official community connected with its games, Valve should seriously examine whether this conduct is compatible with the standards expected from publishers operating on Steam.

I request a formal review of the incident, the relevant moderation records and the treatment of Turkish users who objected to this decision.

This is not a minor moderation dispute.

It is a question of equal treatment, political neutrality and whether a publisher is allowing ideological bias to dictate how an entire national community is treated.

Please investigate this matter seriously.

If you have ever wanted to experience the sheer thrill of an existential crisis while staring at a colored global map for six consecutive hours, Hearts of Iron IV is the absolute pinnacle of entertainment for you. Marketed as a grand strategy game, it is actually a sophisticated psychological evaluation designed to test precisely how much mental abuse a human being can endure before throwing their computer monitor out the window.

The game begins innocently enough: you pick a nation, dream of historical redemption, and immediately realize you have zero grasp of modern logistics. You spend hours meticulously planning a grand campaign, only to watch your entire armored division freeze and starve in a muddy ditch because a single train line lacked steel. Meanwhile, the naval system defies all known laws of physics and quantum mechanics; you can conquer the Eurasian landmass, but the moment your ships touch water, they vanish into a mysterious black hole.

Furthermore, Paradox Interactive deserves a corporate award for their economic philosophy. Buying the base game is merely a cheap entry ticket to a lifelong subscription of mandatory DLCs. If you want your favorite country to have a unique focus tree, you must continually feed the developer's wallet.

In short, Hearts of Iron IV is a full-time, unpaid logistics internship disguised as a hobby. It teaches you that without a proper railway network, you cannot even survive a Tuesday. Save your sanity and stay away.

MUSTAFA KEMAL ATATÜRK[d] (1881,[e] Selanik - 10 Kasım 1938, İstanbul), Türk mareşal, devlet adamı, yazar, Türk Kurtuluş Savaşı'nın başkomutanı, Türkiye Cumhuriyeti'nin kurucusu ve ilk cumhurbaşkanıdır. Türkiye'yi laik, sanayileşen bir ulusa dönüştüren kapsamlı ilerici reformlar üstlenmiştir.[6] İdeolojik olarak sekülarist ve milliyetçi politikaları ve sosyo-politik teorileri Kemalizm olarak tanınmıştır.[6]

I. Dünya Savaşı sırasında Osmanlı ordusunda görev yapan Atatürk, Çanakkale Cephesi'nde miralaylığa, Sina ve Filistin Cephesi'nde ise Yıldırım Ordular Grubu komutanlığına atandı. Savaşın sonunda, Osmanlı İmparatorluğu'nun yenilgisini izleyen Kurtuluş Savaşı ile simgelenen Anadolu Hareketi'ne öncülük ve önderlik etti. Türk Kurtuluş Savaşı sürecinde Ankara Hükûmeti'ni kurdu, Türk Orduları Başkomutanı olarak Sakarya Meydan Muharebesi'ndeki başarısından dolayı 19 Eylül 1921 tarihinde "gazi" sanını aldı ve mareşallik rütbesine yükseldi. Askerî ve siyasal eylemleriyle İtilaf Devletleri ve destekçilerine karşı yengi kazandı. Savaşın ardından Cumhuriyet Halk Partisini "Halk Fırkası" adıyla kurdu ve ilk genel başkanı oldu. 29 Ekim 1923'te cumhuriyetin ilan edilmesinin ardından cumhurbaşkanı seçildi. 1938'deki ölümüne dek dört dönem bu görevi yürütmüş olup günümüze kadar Türkiye'de en uzun süre cumhurbaşkanlığı yapmış kişidir.[7]

Atatürk; çağdaş, ilerici ve laik bir ulus devlet kurmak için siyasal, ekonomik ve kültürel alanlarda sekülarist ve milliyetçi nitelikte yenilikler gerçekleştirdi. Yabancılara tanınan ekonomik ayrıcalıklar kaldırıldı ve onlara ait üretim araçları ve demir yolları millîleştirildi. Tevhîd-i Tedrîsât Kanunu ile eğitim, Türk hükûmetinin denetimine girdi. Seküler ve bilimsel eğitim esas alındı. Binlerce yeni okul yapıldı. İlköğretim ücretsiz ve zorunlu duruma getirildi. Yabancı okullar devlet denetimine alındı. Köylülerin sırtına yüklenen ağır vergiler azaltıldı. Erkeklerin serpuşlarında ve giysilerinde bazı değişiklikler yapıldı. Takvim, saat ve ölçülerde değişikliklere gidildi. Mecelle kaldırılarak yerine seküler Türk Kanunu Medenisi yürürlüğe konuldu. Kadınların sivil ve siyasal hakları pek çok Batı ülkesinden önce tanındı. Çok eşlilik yasaklandı. Kadınların tanıklığı ve miras hakkı, erkeklerinkiyle eşit duruma getirildi. Benzer olarak, dünyanın çoğu ülkesinden önce olarak Türkiye'de kadınlara ilkin yerel seçimlerde (1930), sonra genel seçimlerde (1934) seçme ve seçilme hakkı tanındı. Ceza ve borçlar hukukunda seküler yasalar yürürlüğe konuldu. Sanayi Teşvik Kanunu kabul edildi. Toprak reformu için çabalandı. Arap harfleri temelli Osmanlı alfabesinin yerine Latin harfleri temelli yeni Türk alfabesi kabul edildi. Halkı okuryazar kılmak için eğitim seferberliği başlatıldı. Üniversite Reformu gerçekleştirildi. Birinci Beş Yıllık Sanayi Planı yürürlüğe konuldu. Sınıf ve durum ayrımı gözeten lakap ve ünvanlar kaldırıldı ve soyadları yürürlüğe konuldu. Bağdaşık ve birleşmiş bir ulus yaratılması için Türkleştirme siyaseti yürütüldü.

Türkiye Cumhuriyeti Devlet Demiryolları, Türk Hava Yolları, Maden Tetkik ve Arama Genel Müdürlüğü, Hıfzıssıhha Enstitüsü, Türkkuşu, Sümerbank, Etibank, Türk Tarih Kurumu, Türk Dil Kurumu, Diyanet İşleri Başkanlığı ve daha birçok kamu kurumu Atatürk tarafından veya Atatürk'ün desteğiyle kuruldu. Yerli tarım, tekstil,[8][9][10] makine, uçak[11][12][13] ve otomobil[14] endüstrilerinin gelişimini destekledi. Tüm bunlara karşın Atatürk'ün hedefleri ile ülkenin sosyopolitik yapısı arasındaki uçurum kapanmadı.[15]

I have been playing Paradox games since the early 2000s, starting with Europa Universalis II, Hearts of Iron III and Victoria II, and I have followed the company and its games ever since. I have played Hearts of Iron IV since its release and have continued to support the franchise throughout the years.

That is precisely why what happened on the official HOI4 Discord is so deeply disappointing and completely unacceptable.

An official moderator banned a player simply for using a historical photograph of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk as their profile picture.

What followed was even more disturbing. Instead of applying a clear and reasonable community rule, the moderator made deeply disrespectful and offensive statements about Atatürk and attempted to justify the moderation action with serious historical accusations and claims that demonstrate an astonishing lack of basic historical knowledge.

This is not responsible community moderation.

There is a fundamental difference between legitimate historical discussion and an official moderator making serious accusations about a historical figure while displaying an apparent lack of understanding of the historical context and chronology involved. Using such claims to justify banning a player makes the situation even more unacceptable.

Atatürk is one of the central historical figures of the period represented in Hearts of Iron IV. He is literally represented in the game itself.

A moderator representing a company whose games are built around history should understand the difference between historical debate, personal interpretation and established historical fact. Personal ignorance should never become an official moderation policy.

What makes this particularly disappointing is that this comes from Paradox Interactive.

Paradox has actively developed and sold content centered around Turkey, including Battle for the Bosporus, and has built a large and loyal Turkish community around its games. There are countless Turkish players who have supported Hearts of Iron IV and Paradox for years. Many of us have bought the game, its expansions and additional content and continue to play it today.

You cannot build and benefit from a community while allowing an official representative to make insulting, inflammatory and historically irresponsible statements about one of the most important figures in that community's history.

And this should not be dismissed as simply a matter of Turkish players being offended.

The underlying issue is much broader: what standards does Paradox expect from people who are given authority over its official communities?

A moderator should enforce clearly established rules, not use their position to push personal interpretations, make serious historical accusations without a proper basis, or punish players because of a historical figure appearing in a profile picture.

There is a clear difference between moderating a community and using moderation powers to impose personal views. The latter has no place in an official community representing a company whose games are built around history.

I expect Paradox management to properly investigate what happened, including the moderator's statements, the relevant moderation logs and the decision to ban the player.

If this conduct is confirmed, the moderator should be removed from the official moderation team. Paradox should also issue a clear public apology for the offensive statements, the historical misinformation and the treatment of the affected player.

I have supported Paradox since the early days of these games because I genuinely value what the studio has created and the community around it. I want to continue supporting them.

I am not asking for special treatment for Turkish players, nor am I asking for Atatürk to be exempt from historical criticism.

I am asking for basic historical competence, consistent moderation, accountability and respect.

Paradox should not allow the ignorance and misconduct of one moderator to damage the relationship it has built with its players.

Investigate what happened. Correct the misinformation. Hold the responsible moderator accountable. Apologize to the affected community.

That is the minimum that should be expected from a company whose games are built on history.

While Hearts of Iron IV has a lot of potential, it ultimately becomes an incredibly frustrating experience due to Paradox's classic flaws and business model.

The biggest issue is the predatory DLC policy. The base (vanilla) game feels completely barebones and unfinished. Crucial mechanics like espionage, naval combat reworks, and unique national focus trees for key countries are locked behind dozens of expensive expansions. To get the actual, full experience, you have to spend a small fortune.

Another major problem is the late-game performance. While everything runs smoothly in 1936, by the time you reach 1943 or 1944, the game slows down to a slideshow. The AI spams thousands of useless divisions and makes endless meaningless calculations, crippling the engine. Even on a high-end system, the game's speed crawls to a halt right when the war is supposed to be at its peak.

Speaking of the AI, it is an absolute disaster. Your allies will frequently abandon critical frontlines, drain your supply by stacking millions of troops in one tile, or ruin your carefully planned strategies with their incompetence. And don't even get me started on the peace conferences—the AI creates atrocious "border gore" that completely ruins the map and the immersion.

Overall, unless you have hundreds of dollars to spend on DLCs, infinite patience for terrible late-game lag, and the tolerance to babysit brain-dead AI allies, I cannot recommend this game.

This incident is a perfect example of how absurd moderation can become.
Punishing someone simply because they use Atatürk as their profile picture under the excuse of him being a “controversial figure” is not community moderation. It is an attempt to dictate what people are allowed to represent. The fact that a historical figure is viewed differently in different countries is completely normal. But using that as a reason to police people's profile pictures—especially without a clear and consistently enforced standard—is a serious moderation problem.
And this is the Hearts of Iron IV community. The game itself directly features some of the most controversial political and military figures in modern history, from Mussolini and Churchill to Stalin and Hitler. In a community built around historical figures, wars, and political ideologies, stretching the concept of “controversial historical figure” to someone's profile picture makes this decision even harder to justify.
If you genuinely believe that “no controversial historical figure may be used as a profile picture,” then prove that you enforce this rule equally. If you cannot demonstrate that, people are naturally going to ask: “Why is this rule being enforced here?”
Moderating a community does not mean policing which historical figures people respect or admire. Moderators should be dealing with harassment, threats, hate speech, and behavior that actually harms the community. Treating someone's historical profile picture as if it were a threat is not reasonable moderation—it is an excessive and disproportionate response.
People do not have to share your interpretation of history. Someone expressing admiration for Atatürk through a profile picture does not inherently harm anyone. If you still choose to punish them for it, then at the very least, clearly explain which rule you are enforcing, why you are enforcing it, and demonstrate that the same standard is applied to everyone.
Otherwise, what you have is not “neutral moderation.” It is the arbitrary interpretation of vague rules.For an official game community, the bare minimum should be clear rules, consistent enforcement, and transparency.

Hearts of Iron IV: A World War II Torture

If you have too much free time in your life, extra money burning a hole in your wallet, and you enjoy inflicting unnecessary pain upon yourself, Hearts of Iron IV is the perfect game for you. This logistics simulation, presented by Paradox Interactive under the guise of "Grand Strategy," resembles a color-coded Microsoft Excel spreadsheet far more than it does a video game.

Here are the main reasons why you should stay away from this game:

1. Not a Learning Curve, but a Learning Wall
The game has a tutorial section, but it doesn't go beyond aimlessly clicking around in Ethiopia with the Italian army, and it absolutely never explains the remaining 99% of the game to you. When you first launch it, hundreds of menus, graphs, and incomprehensible numbers are hurled at your screen. Probably not even the developers fully understand how the Naval Combat system actually works. Just to properly design a tank division and deploy it to the frontline, you need to watch 4-hour tutorial videos on YouTube. You are studying instead of playing a game.

2. An Out-of-Control DLC Hell
When you buy the base game, you are essentially just getting a demo or a bare skeleton. Core military and political mechanics—like the espionage system, ship designing, tank designing, or interacting with your allies—are locked behind DLCs. To experience a truly playable and deep game, you are forced to pay a fortune for Paradox's never-ending expansion packs.

3. The Late-Game Disaster
The game starts off quite smoothly and enjoyably in 1936. However, by the time the year reaches 1943, the game engine literally collapses. Because completely irrelevant countries across the globe (like El Salvador or Honduras) pointlessly spam hundreds of makeshift divisions and shuffle them around the map, the game slows down to a crawl even on top-tier processors. Rather than trying to win the war, you start praying that your computer doesn't freeze.

4. Schizophrenic AI
The frontline mechanic is a ticking time bomb with a mind of its own. You draw a flawless defensive line on the map, but the AI suddenly decides to take your 10 most critical divisions and send them to the peak of a mountain on the opposite side of the map where there is absolutely zero danger. Before you even notice, the enemy slips through that gap and occupies your capital. Furthermore, the "ally" AI seems programmed less to help you and more to completely collapse your supply lines by stacking hundreds of garbage units right on your borders.

It is a test of patience with a deliberately overcomplicated interface that exploits the enthusiasm of history buffs and has zero respect for the player's time and money. If you want a genuine World War II experience, buying a history book will be both far cheaper and infinitely less stressful.

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk[e] (c. 1881[f] – 10 November 1938) was a Turkish field marshal and statesperson who was the founder of the Republic of Turkey and served as its first president from 1923 until his death in 1938. He led sweeping reforms, turning Turkey into an industrialising nation. Ideologically a republican, secularist, and nationalist, his policies and socio-political theories became known as Kemalism. Atatürk's personality cult and the Kemalist historiography developed around it have had significant and ongoing influences on Turkey's political culture and historical narrative.
Born in Salonica in the Ottoman Empire, Atatürk was early on persecuted for agitating against Sultan Abdul Hamid II's autocracy, joining opposition movements like the Committee of Union and Progress and the Young Turks. He participated in the Young Turk Revolution and the 31 March Incident. Atatürk denounced CUP leadership for encouraging a politicised military –and was subsequently sidelined– as they established a new authoritarian regime. His early military career saw him involved in the Italo-Turkish and Balkan Wars. He rose to prominence with his role in the Defence of Gallipoli during World War I. Following his country's defeat after the war, in the Turkish War of Independence he directed the Turkish National Movement in a nationalist resistance against Turkey's partition among the victorious Allied powers. Establishing the provisional "Ankara government", he achieved a Turkish victory against Greece, Armenia, France, and the United Kingdom, confirmed in the Treaty of Lausanne. During and after the war, the ethnic cleansing of Armenians and Greeks from Anatolia outside of Istanbul, including the Kars region invaded by the Kemalist armies, was largely completed via large-scale massacres, flight, expulsions, and the population exchange between Greece and Turkey. His government subsequently proceeded to abolish the Ottoman sultanate in 1922 and proclaimed the Republic of Turkey in 1923.
As the president of the newly formed Turkish Republic, Atatürk introduced far reaching reforms to build a republican and secular nation-state with a modern, Western facing society. By the mid-1920s, opponents to Atatürk's rule were suppressed as a one-party regime was cemented around him. This included abolishing the Ottoman Caliphate and curtailing religion as part of a larger secularist campaign. The semi-secular Mecelle was replaced by a fully secular civil code. Western cultural mores were encouraged: such as the banning of the fez and certain men's clothing. State-owned enterprises were established, foreign industrial assets were nationalised, and the first five-year plan was implemented. He opened thousands of schools and introduced the Latin-based Turkish alphabet. Turkish women received equal civil and political rights during his presidency. His government carried out a policy of Turkification, trying to create a homogeneous, unified, and above all secular nation under the Turkish banner. Atatürk attempted rapprochement with Iran, Yugoslavia, Iraq, Romania, and Greece, as well as the creation of the Balkan Pact that resisted the expansionist aggressions of Italy and Bulgaria during the interwar period of the 1930s. He died on 10 November 1938 at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul, at the age of 57; he was succeeded as president by his long-time prime minister İsmet İnönü.
Atatürk has been praised for his military accomplishments, nation-building efforts, social and economic reforms, and diplomatic successes, serving as an inspiration to anti-colonial and anti-imperialist movements. He has been condemned for instituting a dictatorship, introducing assimilationist policies that targeted minorities like the Kurds, and continuing a persecution of Christian minorities started by the CUP, while conservative Muslims have criticised his secular agenda. The Turkish Parliament granted him the surname Atatürk in 1934, meaning "Father of the Turks" or "Turk like his ancestors", in recognition of the role he played in building the Turkish Republic.

Hearts of Iron IV, strateji oyunu kılığına girmiş bir Excel tablosunun sekiz yıldır DLC ile şişirilmiş hâli. Oyuna ilk girdiğinizde “İkinci Dünya Savaşı’nı ben yöneteceğim” sanıyorsunuz; birkaç saat sonra kendinizi 47 farklı menüde fabrika, tren, ikmal, tümen şablonu ve anlamsız yüzdeler arasında kaybolurken buluyorsunuz.

Oyunun en büyük başarısı, basit olması gereken her şeyi gereksiz derecede karmaşık; karmaşık olması gereken savaşları ise inanılmaz derecede aptal hâle getirmesi. Cephe çiziyorsun, plan hazırlıyorsun, ordunu yerleştiriyorsun ve sonra yapay zekâ askerlerini sanki özellikle savaşı kaybetmek için programlanmış gibi sağa sola dağıtıyor. General dediğin adam bazen kritik bir cepheyi boşaltıp askerleri dağın başına yığıyor. Sen strateji kurmuyorsun, kendi ordunun yapay zekâsıyla kavga ediyorsun.

Yapay zekâ zaten başlı başına felaket. Müttefik ülkeler limanlarına milyon tane asker yığıp ikmali çökertiyor, anlamsız çıkarmalar yapıyor, cepheleri boş bırakıyor ve sonra bütün bu rezaletin faturasını oyuncu ödüyor. Düşman yapay zekâsını yenmek çoğu zaman “iyi strateji geliştirmek” değil, oyunun hangi saçmalığını nasıl sömüreceğini öğrenmekten ibaret.

Performans desen ayrı rezalet. Oyun ilerledikçe dünya üzerindeki ülkeler binlerce tümen üretmeye başlıyor ve bir noktadan sonra zaman akışı resmen sürünüyor. Bilgisayarın uzaya roket gönderecek güçte olsa bile 1944’e geldiğinde oyun “bir saniye, bütün dünyanın saçma sapan hesaplarını yapıyorum” diye nefes nefese kalıyor.

Bir de DLC meselesi var. Ana oyunda olması gerektiğini düşündüğünüz mekaniklerin önemli bir kısmı yıllar boyunca ayrı paketlere bölünmüş durumda. Yeni ülke odakları, tasarım sistemleri, casusluk, lojistik, donanma mekanikleri derken oyun değil abonelik sistemi satın almış gibi hissediyorsunuz. Üstelik her yeni sistem oyunu daha derin yapmak yerine bazen yalnızca daha fazla menü ve daha fazla mikro yönetim ekliyor.

Donanma sistemi ayrı bir bilim dalı. Oyunu oynamaya değil doktora yapmaya gelmişsiniz gibi onlarca gemi istatistiğini öğrenmeniz gerekiyor. Hava savaşı desen devasa sayılar, bölgeler ve verim yüzdeleriyle dolu. Bir süre sonra insan “Ben savaş mı yönetiyorum, muhasebe departmanı mı?” diye düşünüyor.

En kötüsü de HOI4’ün size özgürlük vaat edip aslında sürekli kendi mekanikleriyle boğuşmaya zorlaması. Tarihi değiştireyim diyorsun, focus tree bekliyorsun. Orduyu geliştireyim diyorsun XP bekliyorsun. Savaşayım diyorsun ikmal yok. İkmal yapayım diyorsun tren yok. Tren yapıyorsun yakıt yok. Yakıt buluyorsun liman kapasitesi yok. Her şeyin önünde başka bir sayaç, başka bir ceza, başka bir bekleme süresi var.

Kısacası Hearts of Iron IV bazen strateji oyunu değil, oyuncunun sabrını ölçmek için hazırlanmış devasa bir bürokrasi simülatörü gibi. Öğrenmesi saatler, düzgün oynaması yüzlerce saat, sinir olmanız ise yaklaşık 15 dakika sürüyor. “Bir ülkeyi yönetmenin zorluğunu hissettiriyor” denebilir ama bana göre daha çok kötü tasarlanmış menülerle kavga etmenin zorluğunu hissettiriyor.

10 üzerinden puan vermiyorum; çünkü HOI4 oynadıktan sonra sayılara karşı da bir süre tahammülünüz kalmıyor.

Hearts of Iron IV is one of the most frustrating strategy games I have ever played. It feels less like entertainment and more like a test of patience. The AI has no idea what it is doing, allies constantly make ridiculous decisions, the front-line system behaves unpredictably, and instead of managing a war, you end up fixing the game's mistakes.

The DLC system feels like a complete money grab. It constantly feels like you need to buy additional content just to get a proper experience. Despite years of updates and new content, the same fundamental problems keep coming back, which is simply unacceptable.

Performance is another disaster. As the game progresses, everything slows down, waiting times get longer, and you end up staring at the clock while the game struggles to advance through each day. Instead of playing a strategy game, it feels like you're watching your computer change the date.

The micromanagement completely kills the fun as well. You are constantly dealing with units, front lines, and pointless orders. Eventually, you're not even playing strategically anymore—you are just trying to deal with the problems the game keeps throwing at you.

With the poor AI, tedious interface, questionable balance, performance issues, and endless micromanagement, the whole experience becomes exhausting. To me, Hearts of Iron IV feels less like a strategy game and more like a test of patience and frustration. I don't think the time I spent on it was worth it, and I'd rather play literally anything else than open this game again.

Banning Mustafa Kemal Atatürk as a profile picture by labeling him a “controversial figure” over the events of 1915 is historically highly questionable.

It is true that Mustafa Kemal was a member of the Committee of Union and Progress in his younger years. However, by 1909 he was openly criticizing the organization’s involvement in politics and arguing that the military should remain separate from political affairs.

More importantly, when the Armenian deportations were carried out in 1915, Mustafa Kemal was not one of the policymakers responsible for that decision. He spent most of 1915 as a frontline commander at Gallipoli, defending Ottoman territory against the Allied invasion.

So the logic of “he was once a member of the CUP, therefore he can be associated with the events of 1915” is not serious historical reasoning. It ignores chronology, individual responsibility, and Mustafa Kemal’s actual role at the time.

I also do not accept the characterization of the events of 1915 as “genocide,” because I do not believe the available historical evidence sufficiently proves that the Ottoman central government had the specific intent to physically destroy Armenians as an ethnic group.

Regardless of that wider historical debate, one fact remains: there is no established evidence that Atatürk was a decision-maker in the planning or implementation of the 1915 deportation policy.

If a gaming community wants to ban images of historical political figures, it should do so through a clear and consistently applied rule. But banning Atatürk by inaccurately associating him with a policy he did not formulate or direct is something entirely different.

If history is going to be invoked as justification, then chronology and evidence should come first.

Paradox should correct the historically misleading accusations made against Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and take an institutional position regarding the conduct of the moderator responsible.

A moderator of the official Hearts of Iron IV Discord reportedly justified banning an Atatürk profile picture by describing Mustafa Kemal Atatürk as a “controversial figure,” claiming that he “was a member of the Committee of Union and Progress during the Armenian Genocide,” and suggesting that his involvement in or support for those events is disputed.

There are several serious problems with this justification.

First and foremost, the characterization of the events of 1915 as “genocide” is itself a matter of historical, political, and legal dispute. Presenting this characterization, without even acknowledging the existence of opposing positions, as an unquestionable and universally accepted fact reflects a one-sided approach. An official community moderator should not adopt one side of a disputed historical issue as unquestionable truth and then use that position as the basis for punitive moderation.

More importantly, regardless of how the events of 1915 are characterized, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk was not one of the political decision-makers responsible for the deportation policy. Mustafa Kemal had serious disagreements with the political leadership of the Committee of Union and Progress years before 1915 and had distanced himself from its political leadership. In 1915, he was serving as an Ottoman military officer and commanding troops at Gallipoli.

If Paradox or its moderators possess credible historical evidence demonstrating that Mustafa Kemal personally decided, organized, directed, participated in, or supported the deportation or killing of Armenians in 1915, they should present that evidence. Otherwise, such a serious allegation should not be used as a justification for banning his portrait. Attempting to associate Atatürk with these events in order to justify such a ban is historically misleading and entirely irrelevant to the moderation decision.

It is not the place of a Paradox Discord moderator to casually declare Mustafa Kemal Atatürk a “controversial figure” and turn their own personal historical or political judgment into an official moderation standard. Atatürk is the founder and first President of the Republic of Türkiye and occupies a uniquely important place in the history and identity of the Turkish state. A moderator has the authority to enforce clearly established community rules; that authority does not entitle them to impose their personal political interpretation of history on an entire community or to associate Atatürk with actions for which he was not a political decision-maker.

The international treatment of Atatürk also demonstrates how unreasonable it is to regard an ordinary portrait of him as inherently unacceptable. Anıtkabir, Atatürk's mausoleum in Ankara, is routinely visited by foreign heads of state and government during official visits to Türkiye. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson himself visited Anıtkabir during his official visit to Ankara in 2022. Numerous U.S. Presidents and other international leaders have also paid their respects there.

The statements and conduct attributed to this moderator create a serious perception of hostility and prejudice toward Atatürk and Turkish players. We therefore expect Paradox to treat this as an institutional matter rather than dismissing it as a minor Discord dispute. The moderator's conduct should be investigated, the historical claims used to justify these bans should be reviewed, and any inaccurate claims should be corrected. If Paradox's investigation finds bias or violations of its moderation standards, appropriate institutional action should be taken against the person responsible.

This is particularly disturbing coming from a company whose products are built around history and which has a significant Turkish player base. Historical moderation should, at the very least, be based on historical facts rather than the personal political views and prejudices of individual moderators.

Paradox should publicly clarify whether an ordinary portrait of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk is actually prohibited under its community rules, review any bans imposed on this basis, correct the misleading historical claims made by members of its moderation team, and explain what institutional action it intends to take regarding this incident.

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk is not a political label for an individual moderator to redefine at will. He is the founder of the Republic of Türkiye. Turkish players deserve the same respect for their history and national figures that Paradox would be expected to show to any other community.

Paradox Interactive's recent treatment of Turkish players and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk is unacceptable.

I have played Hearts of Iron IV for years, and this negative review is not about the game itself. It is about something much more serious: the way the official community has treated Turkish players and the founder of the Republic of Türkiye.

A Turkish player was banned from the official Hearts of Iron IV Discord server for using a real photograph of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk as his profile picture. During the appeal process, the moderator stated that Atatürk was considered a “controversial figure” and that real-life images of such figures were not permitted. The justification was then connected to the events of 1915 and Atatürk's historical relationship with the Committee of Union and Progress. The moderation team later described Atatürk, alongside figures such as Karl Marx, as a “controversial and polarizing” figure connected to modern politics.

This raises a very simple question:

Why is an ordinary photograph of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, by itself, considered a moderation violation?

Atatürk was the founder of the Republic of Türkiye and the commander who led the Turkish national struggle. His political legacy is also strongly associated with the principle “Peace at home, peace in the world.” Official Turkish historical sources describe his foreign-policy approach as fundamentally oriented toward peace while recognizing war as necessary when the nation's independence and existence were under threat. His well-known statement that, unless a nation's existence is threatened, war is “murder,” reflects that distinction.

An ordinary photograph of such a historical figure does not constitute hate speech, racial hatred, a call for violence, or support for atrocities.

If Paradox's rule is genuinely that real-life photographs of “controversial historical figures” are prohibited, then the obvious expectation is that the rule should be applied consistently to historical figures from every country and every community.

What makes this situation particularly disturbing is that the moderator did not simply enforce a neutral rule. The explanation specifically brought Atatürk into the discussion of the events of 1915 and used that historical controversy to justify treating his image differently.

I am not asking Paradox to give Turkish players special treatment.

I am asking for equal treatment.

Turkish players should not be expected to hide the founder of their own republic in order to participate in an official community while other players are allowed to represent their own historical figures under different standards.

And when Turkish users challenged the decision, reports also emerged of posts and appeals being removed or hidden, users being banned, and the official Discord subsequently being closed to new members. These developments have been reported by multiple sources covering the incident.

This is why I consider this more than an isolated Discord moderation incident.

It raises a serious question about whether Turkish players are being treated according to the same standards as everyone else.

If Atatürk is prohibited because he is supposedly a “controversial historical figure,” then show us the written rule.

If the rule applies equally to everyone, demonstrate that.

If the historical claims used to justify the decision are being made by an official moderator, then those claims should be historically defensible.

And if the bans against Turkish users were unrelated to their nationality or their defense of Atatürk, then Paradox should clearly explain the specific rules that were violated.

No special treatment. No collective guilt. No double standards.

Just the same rules, the same evidence, and the same respect for every player.

Paradox Interactive should publicly address this incident, review the moderation decisions involved, and make it clear that Turkish players are not treated differently because of their nationality or their history.

Until that happens, I cannot recommend supporting this game or Paradox's community practices.

I am adding Paradox Interactive to my personal boycott list.

The recent situation surrounding the Hearts of Iron IV community, where users were reportedly banned or told to change their profile pictures for using an image of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, is deeply disappointing and genuinely concerning.

What makes this worse is the historical reasoning that has apparently been used to justify it. Attempting to associate Atatürk with the events of 1915 in order to label him a “controversial” figure demonstrates a shocking lack of historical nuance from people moderating the community of a company whose games are built around history.

Let me also be very clear about my own position, because I do not accept the genocide characterization of the 1915 events.

I view the deportation policy within the context of a collapsing empire fighting a catastrophic war on several fronts, facing Russian invasion, armed rebellion, intercommunal violence and attacks on Muslim civilians. In those circumstances, I believe the Ottoman government had legitimate security concerns and that some form of population relocation from strategically sensitive areas could be justified as a wartime measure.

That does not mean I celebrate or dismiss the suffering of innocent Armenian civilians. Civilian deaths are tragic regardless of ethnicity. But acknowledging civilian suffering is not the same thing as accepting a particular historical or legal interpretation of why those deaths occurred.

The Ottoman Empire of 1915 was not a wealthy, modern state with the administrative, logistical and humanitarian capacity of today's developed countries. This was an empire in which its own soldiers and Muslim civilian population were also dying in enormous numbers from war, hunger, disease and displacement. That historical reality matters when judging what happened and why.

People are free to disagree with that interpretation. Historical debate is legitimate. What is not legitimate, in my view, is lazily attaching responsibility for 1915 to Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

During the main period of the 1915 deportations, Mustafa Kemal was fighting at Gallipoli. He was not part of the political leadership responsible for designing that policy. Whatever disagreements exist regarding later Turkish-Armenian history, treating Atatürk as though he were personally responsible for the events of 1915 is historically careless.

The hypocrisy becomes even more obvious considering the subject matter of Hearts of Iron itself. Your game contains Hitler, Stalin, Mussolini, Hirohito, Churchill and many other leaders associated with some of the most controversial events in modern history. If simply being a “controversial historical figure” is enough to make an ordinary photograph unacceptable, then that rule should logically apply to an enormous portion of the historical figures represented in your own games.

Historical figures should absolutely be open to criticism. Atatürk is no exception. But criticism should be based on what a person actually did, not on vague associations, historical ignorance or guilt by proximity.

For a company that makes money selling historical grand-strategy games, I expect a far higher standard of historical understanding than this.

Because of the way this situation has been handled, I am adding Paradox Interactive to my boycott list. I will request refunds for every Paradox title I am still eligible to refund, and I will not purchase future Paradox games or DLC unless this issue is properly addressed.

You have lost a customer not because someone criticized Atatürk, but because of the ignorance and double standards demonstrated in the way this situation was handled.

Calling Atatürk a controversial character by stating the fact that he was a member of Committee of Unity and Progress during the events of 1915 is not historical analysis, but conflation of different circumstances.

Yes, Mustafa Kemal was indeed a member of the Committee of Union and Progress in his youth. There is no need to lie about that. Nevertheless, he also promoted the idea of keeping the military away from politics, fought with the leaders of CUP, and was not part of their ruling core. The debate about his role in the CUP is another controversial topic of history.

Thus, there is a significant difference between the statements "he had a connection with Committee of Union and Progress at one point" and "he was associated with Committee of Union and Progress, so it is better to ban his profile picture".

If you want to have a debate about historical figures, fine, have it. Criticize them, quote sources, and present your case. But do not accuse people of something that they never admitted doing. Banning a user's picture due to controversy is not historical moderation, but imposing a moderation policy upon history.

Paradox games are literally about history, so the bare minimum courtesy you can give to a community of historical strategy games enthusiasts is to have a respectful discussion of history and not label people with terms such as "controversial".

In short, no one is arguing about Atatürk's connections with CUP in the past. Nevertheless, claiming that those connections somehow make him responsible for events of 1915 is sheer nonsense unless you have any evidence besides his name on the same document as the people actually doing the nasty stuff.

I can no longer recommend this game, nor do I feel comfortable supporting Paradox Interactive while the recent treatment of the Turkish community on its official community platforms remains unaddressed.

The recent moderation controversy surrounding Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and first President of the Republic of Türkiye, is deeply disappointing. Turkish users have reported being penalized for using Atatürk’s portrait as a profile picture, while a moderation response reportedly characterized him as a controversial figure and attempted to associate him with the events of 1915.

For millions of Turkish people, Atatürk is not simply a random historical or political figure. He is the founder of the Republic of Türkiye and an enormously important part of our country’s history and national identity. Turkish players therefore have every right to be angered when his image is treated as grounds for moderation and when serious historical accusations are used to justify that decision.

More importantly, historical claims of this magnitude should not be casually presented by community moderators as justification for banning users. Atatürk was serving as an Ottoman military officer and commander during the First World War and was fighting at Gallipoli in 1915. Associating his portrait with atrocities for the purpose of moderating a Turkish player’s profile is, at the very least, a serious historical claim that demands far greater care, evidence and consistency than what appears to have been demonstrated here.

The reaction to the incident is also concerning. Turkish community members have reported deleted objections, moderation actions against users challenging the decision, and inconsistent treatment of different historical figures. Whether every individual allegation ultimately proves correct should be established through a transparent investigation, but the material already circulating within the community is serious enough that silence is not an adequate response.

This is not about demanding special treatment for Turkish players. It is about demanding equal treatment.

If portraits of historical figures are permitted, the rules should be applied consistently regardless of nationality. If historical discussion is permitted, moderators should not selectively enforce controversial interpretations as unquestionable fact. And if a moderator makes a serious historical accusation while acting in an official community, Paradox should be willing to review that conduct openly and fairly.

I have supported Paradox games because I enjoy grand strategy and history. That makes this situation particularly disappointing. A company whose games are built around history should understand better than most how sensitive historical subjects can be and how important accuracy, neutrality and consistency are when moderating an international community.

My negative review is therefore not directed at the developers, artists or designers who worked on this individual game. It reflects my decision as a customer not to financially support Paradox Interactive while this incident remains unresolved.

I expect Paradox Interactive to investigate what happened, clarify its moderation standards, address the treatment of Turkish players, correct any demonstrably false historical claims used in moderation decisions, and take appropriate action if its rules were applied improperly.

Until then, I cannot recommend this game.

Respect is not something Turkish players should have to beg for.

We are customers, we are members of this community, and we deserve the same standards of fairness and respect as everyone else.

I have supported Hearts of Iron IV for years, but the way Turkish players are currently being treated in parts of this community has seriously damaged my opinion of Paradox and the people representing this game.

A Turkish player was banned from the HOI4 Discord during a dispute involving his profile picture of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and first President of the Republic of Türkiye. Atatürk was then described as a “controversial” figure and dragged into accusations concerning the events of 1915.

Atatürk was not the Ottoman political authority directing government policy in 1915. He was a military officer commanding the 19th Division at Gallipoli, years before he founded the Republic of Türkiye and became its first President in 1923. Trying to turn an ordinary photograph of Atatürk into hateful or extremist imagery by associating him with those events is completely unjustified.

What makes this absolutely indefensible is the blatant double standard.

There are people in the same Discord openly using pictures of Stalin without being banned. Yet Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder of modern Türkiye, whose entire Republican foreign-policy doctrine was built around “Peace at Home, Peace in the World”, is apparently so “controversial” that a Turkish player can be banned over his portrait.

Think about the absurdity of that standard.

Atatürk was respected even by former enemies of Türkiye. Eleftherios Venizelos, the former Greek Prime Minister whose country had fought against Atatürk's forces only years earlier, went on to nominate Atatürk for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1934 for his contribution to peace and Greek-Turkish reconciliation.

And this is the man a Hearts of Iron IV moderator decided was too “controversial” for a profile picture while Stalin portraits remain acceptable?

No. I am not going to pretend that this looks neutral.

When Turkish players are subjected to a restriction that is plainly not being applied to comparable or vastly more extreme historical figures from other countries, and when the people objecting to that treatment have their messages removed and are themselves banned, I consider that anti-Turkish and racist moderation.

Atatürk is not some fringe political symbol that Turkish people are expected to quietly distance themselves from whenever somebody else finds him inconvenient. He is the founder of our Republic. His surname, Atatürk, literally means “Father of the Turks.”

For Turks, Atatürk is not a bargaining chip.

We are not going to take one step back from him because a Discord moderator has decided that displaying the founder of our own country is somehow unacceptable.

This is especially ridiculous in Hearts of Iron IV, a game built around twentieth-century nations, governments, leaders, ideologies and history. Atatürk is literally part of the historical period represented by the game.

Turkish players challenged this treatment. Their messages were removed or hidden. People were banned. The Discord was subsequently closed to new joins. When the issue was taken to Steam, criticism was again suppressed instead of the underlying double standard being answered.

Deleting criticism does not answer it.

Banning the people pointing out the double standard does not make the double standard disappear.

If Paradox believes this moderation was justified, then explain it publicly.

Explain exactly what rule makes an ordinary Atatürk portrait bannable.

Explain why Stalin portraits are acceptable under that same rule.

Explain why Turkish players challenging the decision were banned.

Explain why their responses were removed.

And explain why the founder of the Turkish Republic is apparently subjected to a standard that other countries' historical figures are not.

Turkish players are not second-class members of this community. We bought the same game, support the same company and participate in the same community as everybody else.

We do not need special treatment.

We demand equal treatment.

And we are certainly not going to erase Atatürk from our identity to satisfy discriminatory moderation.

Until Paradox addresses this properly, I cannot recommend supporting Hearts of Iron IV.

No anti-Turkish double standards.
No discriminatory moderation.
Not a single step back.

Same rules. Same evidence. Same standards. Same respect.

This negative review is not about balance, DLC pricing, bugs, or game mechanics.

It is about Paradox’s treatment of the Turkish community and the completely unacceptable handling of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

What we are seeing right now feels like blatant selective moderation. Turkish players, Turkish-themed mods, and content involving Atatürk are being scrutinized and punished while organized pressure campaigns against Turkish historical representation appear to be taken far more seriously than the concerns of the Turkish community itself.

Atatürk is not some obscure fictional character that Paradox can casually disrespect or erase to satisfy whoever complains the loudest. He is the founder of the Republic of Türkiye and one of the most important figures in modern Turkish history.

If Paradox wants to sell a historical grand-strategy game to Turkish players, take our money through countless DLCs, use Turkish history as game content, and profit from a massive Turkish player base, then the absolute minimum expectation is basic historical respect and consistent moderation.

The worst part is the treatment of the modding community.

Mods are one of the main reasons Hearts of Iron IV has remained relevant for this long. Going after Turkish mods or creators while appearing to bend under politically motivated pressure sends an extremely ugly message: some communities are apparently allowed to organize complaints and dictate what is acceptable, while Turkish players are expected to stay silent and accept it.

We will not.

This is not about demanding propaganda. It is not about asking Paradox to rewrite history in Türkiye's favor. It is about applying the same standards to everyone and not treating Turkish historical figures, Turkish creators, or the Turkish community as disposable whenever controversy appears.

Paradox needs to clearly explain what happened, restore or reconsider content that was unfairly targeted, stop selective enforcement against Turkish mods and creators, and establish transparent moderation standards that apply equally to every community.

Until then, I cannot recommend Hearts of Iron IV.

A strategy game built around history should show more respect for history — and for the community that has supported it for years.

It is not merely laughable, but downright sickening hypocrisy that those sitting in the management seat of a history-based strategy game are so hopelessly ignorant of history. For a platform like Hearts of Iron IV—which allows players to control the bloodiest dictators of World War II, fascist regimes, and the imperialist powers that set the world on fire—to declare Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, a leader who dedicated his life to fighting imperialism, a "controversial figure" is the clearest proof of a pathetic double standard.

What is happening here is digital bullying driven by blatant Turkophobia, cowardly hiding behind the guise of "community guidelines." This is not moderation; it is a hate crime.

Attempting to associate a leader with so-called genocide claims—a leader who was fighting a war of survival against imperialist armies at Gallipoli in 1915, and whose deep political and military conflicts with the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP) leadership are well-documented in world history—cannot be explained away as simple ignorance. This is the audacity of incompetent moderators who are incapable of reading history, attempting to spew their personal ideologies and venom on a platform where they hold power. The fact that the official representatives of a supposedly "historical strategy" game have committed such a colossal historical blunder completely nullifies the game's own credibility.

Here lies the absolute peak of hypocrisy: In an ecosystem where it is perfectly acceptable to play with the portraits of figures responsible for the slaughter of millions, actual genocides, and massacres—such as Adolf Hitler, Joseph Stalin, Hirohito, or Benito Mussolini—and where promoting these ideologies is freely permitted under the excuse of "game mechanics" and "historical simulation," banning the founder of a nation is not impartiality; it is sheer delusion. This censorship is not designed to protect the community; it is a deliberate operation intended to impose a twisted, fabricated history upon Turkish players.

Paradox Interactive claims to sell "Historical Grand Strategy," yet it has surrendered its official channels to a mob that twists historical facts with baseless slanders and blatantly commits racism by targeting a specific nation. This disgraceful decision reveals not only the profound ignorance of those authorities, but also how recklessly they exploit every opportunity to legitimize their hatred.

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's legacy of bringing imperialism to its knees and his historical reality are far too immense to be erased by the "ban" button of a few clueless moderators who think they can rewrite history from behind a keyboard. What will actually be erased is the credibility of these cheap censors who try to disguise their hatred as "rules," and the company that turns a blind eye to them.

Hearts of Iron IV is an absolute nightmare of a game. What should be an engaging World War II grand strategy title is instead a frustrating, tedious, and bloated exercise in menu management.
The computer-controlled nations are incomprehensibly dumb. Your allies will constantly flood your frontlines, completely destroying your supply networks and starving your troops, while enemy armies frequently pull off suicidal naval invasions or leave entire borders completely unguarded. To make matters worse, the base game feels like a gutted, empty shell because core mechanics are locked behind a paywall of endless, expensive DLCs.
The battle planner system is a total disaster. Assign an army to a frontline, and the game will happily shuffle divisions back and forth across an entire continent, burning through all their supply and equipment for no reason while the enemy simply walks through your open line. Once you reach 1943, the performance grinds to an agonizing halt as the AI spams hundreds of useless division templates, melting your CPU and making every single day take an eternity to pass. Instead of actual strategic depth, you are left with convoluted UI clutter and unexplained numbers that force you to read third-party wikis for hours.
It is less of a grand strategy game and more of a glorified spreadsheet simulator where you spend ten hours setting up factories just to watch the AI ruin your entire plan in five seconds. Avoid it unless you enjoy pure frustration.

For a game that has been around for over 10 years, HOI4 has an absurdly expensive DLC model.

Too many mechanics that should be fundamental parts of the base game are locked behind paid DLC. Instead of expanding the game with optional content, Paradox has gradually turned essential gameplay features into additional purchases. Getting the complete experience can cost hundreds of dollars.

And after all that spending, the technical performance is still unacceptable. Even on modern hardware, performance can deteriorate badly after 1940s, with stuttering, freezes, and severe slowdowns.

The AI is no better. After more than a decade of development, it still has countless exploitable weaknesses. Many popular meta strategies are built around abusing AI behavior rather than genuine strategic depth.

What makes the DLC model even harder to defend is that many of these mechanics are based on ideas that have existed in free community mods for years—and some of those mods are more stable than the official content.

And then there is Paradox's treatment of historical figures. Calling Mustafa Kemal Atatürk a “controversial figure” was deeply disrespectful to millions of Turkish players. The backlash was entirely predictable.

Add that to the overpriced DLC model, poor optimization, and decade-old AI problems, and it's hard to see much respect for the players behind this game.

Paylaşılan ekran görüntüleri, Steam’deki tartışmalar ve Paradox tarafından verilen açıklamalara göre, profil fotoğrafında Mustafa Kemal Atatürk’ün gerçek bir fotoğrafını kullanan Türk bir oyuncudan bu fotoğrafı değiştirmesi istendi ve sunucuya erişimi bu mesele nedeniyle kısıtlandı. Paradox temsilcisi de resmî Discord’da “tartışmalı sayılabilecek kişilerin” profil fotoğrafı olarak kullanılmamasına yönelik bir kural bulunduğunu ve oyuncudan Atatürk fotoğrafını değiştirmesinin istendiğini doğruladı. 

Ben bir Türk oyuncu olarak bu yaklaşımı kabul etmiyorum.

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk’ün 1915 üzerinden suçlayıcı bir çerçeve içerisinde değerlendirilmesini tarihsel açıdan yanlış ve Türk toplumuna karşı son derece saygısız buluyorum. Ayrıca kendi okuduğum kaynaklar ve tarih anlayışım doğrultusunda, 1915’te yaşananların “Ermeni Soykırımı” olarak nitelendirilmesini kabul etmiyorum. Bu benim tarihî görüşümdür. Başkalarının farklı düşünme hakkına saygı duyduğum gibi, benim de bu nitelendirmeyi reddetme hakkım olduğunu düşünüyorum. Bir oyun şirketinin veya moderasyon ekibinin böylesine tartışmalı tarih meselelerinde tek bir yorumu bütün kullanıcılar için zorunlu bir doğru hâline getirmemesi gerekir.

İttihat ve Terakki konusu da benim açımdan bir hakaret veya utanılması gereken bir geçmiş değildir. Mustafa Kemal gençlik yıllarında İttihat ve Terakki üyesiydi; daha sonraki yıllarda cemiyetin yönetimi ve siyasi çizgisiyle ciddi fikir ayrılıkları yaşayarak bu yapıdan uzaklaştı.  Ben şahsen Türk milliyetçisiyim ve İttihat ve Terakki’ye, özellikle Enver Paşa, Talat Paşa ve Cemal Paşa’ya büyük saygı duyuyorum. Hatta tarihî ve siyasi açıdan kendimi İttihat ve Terakki geleneğine Atatürk’ten daha yakın hissediyorum. Bunun herkes tarafından paylaşılması gereken bir görüş olduğunu iddia etmiyorum; bunlar benim şahsi tarihî ve siyasi görüşlerimdir.

Bu nedenle Atatürk’ün İttihat ve Terakki geçmişinin veya 1915 tartışmasının, gerçek bir Atatürk fotoğrafını yasaklamak için gerekçe hâline getirilmesini kabul etmiyorum. Aynı şekilde bir insanın Atatürk’e, İttihat ve Terakki’ye veya Üç Paşalara olumlu bakması da kendi başına nefret söylemi olarak değerlendirilemez. İnsanların bu tarihî şahsiyetler hakkında olumlu veya olumsuz görüş bildirmesi tartışmanın bir parçası olabilir; çözüm insanların profil fotoğraflarını yasaklamak veya onları topluluktan uzaklaştırmak olmamalıdır.

Paradox’un ayrıca Türkiye’de ve Türkiye ile ilgili içeriklere ilgi gösteren oyuncular arasında ne kadar güçlü bir karşılığı olduğunu da dikkate alması gerektiğini düşünüyorum. Ben de Hearts of Iron IV ve diğer Paradox oyunlarını oynayan Türk oyunculardan biriyim. Paradox’un kendi verilerinde bile Türkiye, yeniden düzenlenmeden önce Hearts of Iron IV’ün en çok oynanan küçük ülkesi olarak belirtilmiş; Battle for the Bosporus’un çıkışından hemen sonra ise oynanan ülkeler içerisinde %16 ile ikinci sıraya yükselmiştir. 

Türk oyuncular yıllardır Paradox oyunlarını satın alıyor, DLC’lerine para ödüyor, modlar ve rehberler hazırlıyor, topluluklar oluşturuyor ve bu oyunların etrafındaki ekosistemin aktif bir parçası oluyor. Ben de bu oyunculardan biriyim. Bu nedenle Paradox’un resmî topluluklarında Türk oyuncuların tarihî ve kültürel hassasiyetlerinin küçümsenmemesi gerektiğini düşünüyorum.

Kimsenin Atatürk’ü, İttihat ve Terakki’yi, Üç Paşaları veya 1915’i benimle aynı şekilde değerlendirmesini istemiyorum. Bizim talep ettiğimiz özel muamele de değildir. Talep ettiğimiz şey, Türk oyuncular için de aynı ifade özgürlüğünün, aynı saygının ve aynı moderasyon standartlarının uygulanmasıdır.

Bu olaya tepki gösteren Türk oyuncu topluluğu olarak Paradox’tan konuyu ciddiyetle ve şeffaf biçimde incelemesini, yapılan hatadan derhal dönmesini, bu olay nedeniyle uygulanmış haksız yaptırımlar varsa kaldırmasını ve Türk oyuncu topluluğundan açık, doğrudan ve resmî bir özür dilemesini bekliyoruz.

Bunun küçük bir moderasyon hatası olarak geçiştirilmesini doğru bulmuyoruz. Atatürk’ün gerçek bir fotoğrafının bu şekilde sorun hâline getirilmesi ve buna tepki gösteren Türk oyuncuların endişelerinin dikkate alınmaması kabul edilebilir değildir.

Tarih tartışılabilir. Atatürk tartışılabilir. İttihat ve Terakki ve Üç Paşalar tartışılabilir. Benim görüşlerim de tartışılabilir. Fakat tarihî tartışmalara verilecek cevap sansür veya susturma olmamalıdır.

Özel muamele istemiyoruz. Eşit muamele, yapılan hatanın düzeltilmesi ve Türk oyuncu topluluğundan bir özür bekliyoruz.

Tarihi konu alan oyunlar yapan uluslararası bir şirketten beklediğimiz şey, tek bir tarih yorumunu oyuncularına dayatmak değil; farklı görüşlere sahip oyuncularına eşit ve saygılı davranmasıdır.

Hearts of Iron IV has a lot of potential, but the game has several serious problems. The AI can be frustrating and often makes strange decisions, especially during wars. The combat system can also feel unnecessarily complicated and difficult to understand for new players.

Another major issue is the amount of DLC required to get the full experience. The base game feels incomplete compared to the amount of content locked behind additional purchases. The game can also become repetitive after playing for a while, especially if you are not interested in constantly learning new mechanics.

The performance can suffer in the late game as well, with the game slowing down significantly when there are many countries and units on the map.

Overall, HOI4 can be fun, but its weak AI, complicated mechanics, heavy reliance on DLC, and late-game performance issues make it difficult to recommend without reservations.

Hearts of Iron IV is a World War II strategy game that puts countless controversial and authoritarian historical figures at the center of its setting, from Stalin to Mussolini. Yet in the game’s official community, using Mustafa Kemal Atatürk as a profile picture can apparently become an issue because he is considered a “controversial political figure.”

That is an absurd double standard.

If the rule is that political figures are not allowed in the community, fine. Then the same rule should be applied **consistently to every historical figure and every user.**

You can tolerate images of figures such as Stalin and other dictators, then suddenly become extremely strict when the person in question is Atatürk. If the standard changes depending on which historical figure is being discussed, then this is not neutral moderation.

It is also especially disturbing to see Atatürk being framed through accusations related to 1915 and then having that used as justification for moderation decisions in the official community of a historical strategy game.

Deleting criticism, timing users out, or banning people who question these decisions does not solve the problem. It only makes the moderation look even more arbitrary.

Turkish players who have spent hundreds or even thousands of hours playing Paradox games are also part of this community and deserve to be treated with the same standards as everyone else.

I would prefer to judge the game purely on its gameplay. However, the behavior and moderation standards of its official community make it impossible for me to leave a positive review at this time.

**The request is simple: one rule, one standard, applied equally to everyone.**

Until Paradox addresses this inconsistency, I cannot recommend Hearts of Iron IV.

An increasingly expensive game that feels less complete with every DLC

Hearts of Iron IV could be an excellent grand strategy game, but Paradox's DLC model and the game's long-standing technical problems make it increasingly difficult to recommend.

The biggest problem is the DLC system. The base game feels extremely limited compared to the amount of content locked behind DLCs. If you want the complete experience, you are expected to purchase a large number of expansions, and the total cost can become absurdly high. It often feels like you are buying a fraction of a game and then paying repeatedly to unlock the rest.

Performance is another major issue. As the game progresses into the later years, performance can deteriorate significantly, with increasing lag and slowdowns. This is especially frustrating because even players with powerful PCs can experience severe late-game performance problems. Having a high-end computer does not necessarily prevent the game from becoming increasingly sluggish as the timeline advances.

There are also long-standing bugs and technical issues that become more noticeable during extended campaigns. After years of updates and DLC releases, it is disappointing to see the game still suffering from problems that affect the overall experience.

There are also issues with localization and geographical naming that are particularly noticeable to Turkish players. Some provinces within the Republic of Türkiye are displayed using K*rdish names rather than their Turkish names. Regardless of the political or historical debate surrounding these names, the fact that such localization issues have remained in the game for years without being properly addressed is frustrating for Turkish players who expect the map and localization to accurately represent modern Türkiye.

HOI4 has a fantastic foundation, but the combination of an expensive DLC ecosystem, limited base-game content, worsening late-game performance, persistent bugs, and unresolved localization issues makes it increasingly difficult to justify the cost.

I hope Paradox eventually focuses more on improving the core game, fixing long-standing technical problems, optimizing late-game performance, and addressing localization issues instead of continually expanding the DLC catalog.

Cherry Cheesecake Recipe

For the cheesecake base:

200-250 g oatmeal or rye biscuits
60-100 g melted butter
1/2 cup finely ground hazelnuts or walnuts (optional)
Cheesecake Cream:

600 g labneh cheese (with excess water drained)
400 ml liquid cream
1 cup granulated sugar
3 eggs (at room temperature)
3 tablespoons starch (wheat or corn)
1 packet of vanilla
Half a lemon juice and zest
Cherry Sauce:

300 g pitted cherries (fresh or frozen)
5 tablespoons of granulated sugar
1 cup of water
2 tablespoons of starch (dissolved in half a tea glass of water)
Preparation
Prepare the Base: Grind the biscuits into flour using a food processor. Mix with melted butter and hazelnuts. Line the base of the springform pan with parchment paper and press the mixture into the pan. Refrigerate for 10-15 minutes.

Prepare the cream: Whip the labneh and cream in a mixer until smooth. Add sugar, eggs, starch, vanilla, and lemon juice by grating them, then mix briefly. Be careful not to whisk too much, otherwise the cheesecake may crack.

Bake: Pour the cream over the base. Its heart settles on the top of a deep oven and add a tray of water (water bath). Bake in a preheated 180°C oven for 10 minutes, then reduce to 160°C and bake for another 50 minutes. Turn off the oven and let it rest with the door open for 1 hour.

Cherry Sauce: Place the cherries, sugar, and water in a pot; bring to a boil, then add the starch and stir until thickened. Let the sauce cool down.

Serving: When the cheesecake is completely cold, pour it over the cherry sauce. It rests in the refrigerator for at least 4-6 hours, preferably overnight. Serve willingly. Depending on what you want, you can decorate with mint-made or powdered pistachios.
